# Language bindings and the handler execution model

Research notes for the zero-server Rust core. Every claim below is tagged with the source it was fetched from in this task or the measurement that produced it; anything else is marked unverified.

## 1. The owner's established binding pattern (pamoja, read locally)

Read from C:\Users\tonyw\Desktop\projects\zero-edge on 2026-09-29.

### Workspace shape
- Root Cargo workspace (`Cargo.toml`): `crates/pamoja-core`, capability crates, `crates/pamoja-ffi`, `crates/xtask`, `examples`. `bindings/node` and `bindings/python` are excluded from the workspace ("standalone crates with their own toolchains and lint policy; they are built by their own pipelines").
- `[workspace.lints.rust] missing_docs = "deny"`, `unsafe_code = "warn"`; `[workspace.lints.clippy] all = "warn"`; `[profile.release] lto = "thin"`, `codegen-units = 1`.
- `rust-toolchain.toml`: stable channel, components rustfmt and clippy. The local rules file states the local scoop toolchain lacks rustfmt, clippy, and rustup, so fmt and clippy run in the official `rust:latest` Docker image with `CARGO_TARGET_DIR=/tmp/t`.
- `deny.toml`: `exclude-dev = true`, advisories `yanked = "deny"`, license allow list (MIT, Apache-2.0, BSD-2/3, ISC, Unicode-3.0, Zlib), MPL-2.0 exception for cbindgen only, `unknown-registry = "deny"`, `unknown-git = "deny"`.
- Workflows: ci, codeql, node, python, dotnet, release-crates, release-node, release-python, release-nuget, release-github, release-preflight, docs, pages, labels, links, badges, prices, pypi-backfill.
- `conformance/vectors.json` is regenerated by a Rust example in CI and diffed (`git diff --exit-code -- conformance/vectors.json`); Node (`conformance.js`), Python (`tests/test_conformance.py`), and .NET smoke tests read the same vectors.

### Three binding tiers, one shape per language
- Every binding has a "contract tier" (generated, one-to-one with Rust) and a hand-written idiomatic facade.
- Node: `bindings/node` is one napi-rs cdylib (`napi = { version = "3", default-features = false, features = ["napi6", "tokio_rt"] }`, `napi-derive = "3"`, `napi-build = "2"`), built with `napi build --platform --release` into `packages/native` (`@pamoja/native`, targets linux x64/arm64 gnu, darwin x64/arm64, win32 x64 msvc, `engines.node >= 16`). `packages/core` is the TypeScript facade; one `@pamoja/*` package per capability. Every capability is a cargo feature.
- Python: `bindings/python/packages/native` is a PyO3 cdylib+rlib (`pyo3 = { version = "0.29", features = ["abi3-py310"] }`, `pyo3-async-runtimes = { version = "0.29", features = ["tokio-runtime"] }`, `pyo3-stub-gen = "0.23"`), built with maturin (`python-source = "python"`, `module-name = "pamoja._native"`); a `stub_gen` binary regenerates the committed `.pyi`. The facade re-exports the contract as `pamoja.raw`.
- .NET: `crates/pamoja-ffi` is a hand-written `extern "C"` crate (`crate-type = ["lib", "cdylib", "staticlib"]`), header generated by cbindgen (`cbindgen = "0.29"`, `parse_deps = false`, `prefix_with_name = true`) and drift-checked in CI. `bindings/dotnet/src/Pamoja.Native` mirrors `pamoja.h` with `[LibraryImport]` partial methods (`AllowUnsafeBlocks` true in `Directory.Build.props`, net8.0, `TreatWarningsAsErrors`), native binaries packed under `runtimes/<rid>/native/`. `Pamoja.Core` and one `Pamoja.*` project per capability are the facade.

### Conventions worth carrying over verbatim
- Fallible C calls return a status enum; the message is stored thread-locally and read with `pamoja_last_error_message` (ffi `lib.rs`).
- Handles are opaque, heap allocated, caller owned, released with a matching `*_free` (ffi `lib.rs`).
- Host callbacks are a `#[repr(C)]` struct of `Option<unsafe extern "C" fn>` pointers plus `user_data` (`host.rs`); the .NET side fills it with `delegate* unmanaged[Cdecl]<...>` pointing at `[UnmanagedCallersOnly(CallConvs = new[] { typeof(CallConvCdecl) })]` static methods (`HostThunks.cs`, `PamojaTransportCallbacks.cs`); `user_data` is a `GCHandle`.
- Host callbacks that may block run on tokio's blocking pool (`tokio::task::spawn_blocking` in `host.rs`).
- .NET wraps every pointer in a `SafeHandle` subclass (`NativeHandle.cs`) using `DangerousAddRef`/`DangerousRelease`, an optional `SemaphoreSlim` gate to serialize calls, and `LendAsync` for async work.
- Node integer arguments go through a `Whole<T>` checker (`checked.rs`) because `napi_get_value_uint32` silently truncates.
- Node/Python host transports: a `HostTransport` wraps JS/Python objects; Node uses `ThreadsafeFunction` and `Promise`; Python uses `pyo3_async_runtimes::TaskLocals`.
- Observed cost pattern in `HostThunks.Send`: the payload is copied into a fresh `byte[]` (`Marshal.Copy`) on every callback and the topic is decoded with `Marshal.PtrToStringUTF8`; the async result is blocked on with `GetAwaiter().GetResult()`. That is fine for MQTT message rates and wrong for an HTTP hot path; see section 5.

## 2. Node (napi-rs) facts fetched this task

Sources: napi.rs docs (threadsafe-function, typed-array, external, async-fn, async-task), nodejs.org n-api.html and addons.html, github.com/napi-rs/napi-rs README.

- ThreadsafeFunction is the only way to reach JavaScript from another thread: "you can't access napi_env, napi_value, and napi_ref on another thread" (napi.rs threadsafe-function). Call modes `Blocking` (waits for queue space) and `NonBlocking` (returns `Status::QueueFull`); `MaxQueueSize` bounds the queue; `Weak = true` lets the process exit with pending callbacks; `call_with_return_value` and `call_async_catch` bring a return value or a Promise back to Rust. Callback arguments must be `'static`.
- Node-API: "The callback will be called on the main thread"; `napi_call_threadsafe_function` is either `napi_tsfn_nonblocking` or `napi_tsfn_blocking` when the queue is full (nodejs.org n-api).
- Buffers: "Where the runtime permits external buffers, NAPI-RS transfers the allocation to the JavaScript Buffer without a copy, and its finalizer releases the Vec<u8> after JavaScript collects the buffer"; Electron cannot (V8 memory cage) and NAPI-RS copies there. Received buffers get a `napi_ref` that "keeps the JavaScript object and backing store alive until the Rust wrapper is dropped". Borrowed `BufferSlice<'env>` / `Uint8ArraySlice<'env>` are zero-copy and scoped to the call. Owned `Buffer` across threads is a documented data race hazard: "JavaScript can retain and mutate the same backing store while Rust holds a wrapper" (napi.rs typed-array). Node-API exposes `napi_no_external_buffers_allowed` for runtimes that refuse external buffers (nodejs.org n-api).
- `External<T>` is "an empty, blank JavaScript Object that holds the native value under the hood" and "only works by passing the object back to Rust" (napi.rs external). This is the opaque request handle primitive.
- `#[napi] async fn` runs "on the NAPI-RS-managed Tokio runtime and converts the result into a JavaScript Promise"; `&self` in an async method is converted to a `Reference` so GC cannot collect it across an await (napi.rs async-fn). `AsyncTask::compute` runs on the libuv threadpool and `resolve` on the main thread (napi.rs async-task).
- Worker threads: Node-API addons are context-aware by construction; "the bindings it provides may be called multiple times, from multiple contexts, and even concurrently from multiple threads"; per-environment state goes in `napi_set_instance_data`; "Caching the napi_env for the purpose of general reuse, and passing the napi_env between instances of the same addon running on different Worker threads is not allowed" (nodejs.org n-api). Addons must "clean up any resources they may have allocated when such a thread exits" (nodejs.org addons).
- Node-API minimum: napi-rs README says "requires Node@10.0.0 or later"; pamoja pins napi6 for BigInt.
- Measured call overhead: no number is published on the pages fetched. See section 6 for the measurement run here.

## 3. Python (PyO3) facts fetched this task

Sources: pyo3.rs latest (free-threading, parallelism, performance, async-await, calling-existing-code), docs.rs pyo3-async-runtimes.

- Free-threaded CPython: "Since PyO3 0.28, PyO3 defaults to assuming Python modules created with it are thread-safe"; opt out with `#[pymodule(gil_used = true)]`. A module that opts out makes the interpreter re-enable the GIL at runtime with a RuntimeWarning. Under free-threading, "holding a 'py lifetime means only that the thread is currently attached to the Python interpreter; other threads can be simultaneously interacting with the interpreter." `pyclass` data is guarded by runtime borrow checking, so concurrent mutable access raises or panics. "The free-threaded build uses a completely new ABI and there is not yet an equivalent to the limited API for the free-threaded ABI": `abi3` is ignored, version-specific wheels are required. Support arrived in PyO3 0.23.
- GIL parallelism: `Python::detach` (formerly `allow_threads`) releases the interpreter while Rust runs; the guide's benchmark: Rust parallel 1.9972 ms, Rust sequential 8.0035 ms, Rust sequential with Python threading 8.4511 ms, pure Python 28.9604 ms (pyo3.rs parallelism).
- Performance page: "attaching and detaching from the Python interpreter takes less than a millisecond, so any work which is expected to take multiple milliseconds can likely benefit from detaching"; `Bound<'py, T>` gives the token for free while `Python::attach()` "still has a cost"; Rust tuples as call arguments use vectorcall, `Bound<PyTuple>` falls back to `tp_call`; `pyo3_disable_reference_pool` removes the deferred-decref synchronization (pyo3.rs performance).
- Native async: `#[pyfunction] async fn` needs `experimental-async`; "each coroutine.send call is translated to a Future::poll call"; the future stays "attached to the interpreter during the execution of the future" and "there is currently no simple way to detach from the interpreter when awaiting a future"; futures and arguments must be `Send + 'static` (pyo3.rs async-await).
- pyo3-async-runtimes: `future_into_py` and `into_future` are the recommended bridges; "we don't have a way to run Rust futures directly on Python's event loop. Likewise, Python's coroutines cannot be directly spawned on a Rust runtime"; asyncio "needs to have control over the main thread in order to handle signals like CTRL-C correctly"; `TaskLocals` carries the loop and contextvars (docs.rs pyo3-async-runtimes). pamoja already uses this.
- Callback cost: calling a Python callable from Rust requires the attached token and a tuple of arguments (pyo3.rs calling-existing-code); no nanosecond figure is published on the pages fetched. See section 6.

## 4. .NET native interop facts fetched this task

Sources: learn.microsoft.com (pinvoke-source-generation, native-interop/best-practices, csharp unsafe-code, UnmanagedCallersOnlyAttribute, SafeHandle, TaskCompletionSource).

- `[LibraryImport]` (".NET 7 introduces a source generator") replaces the runtime-generated IL stub: "removing the need for the generation of an IL stub at runtime and allowing the P/Invoke to be inlined"; DllImport "isn't an option for platforms that require full Native AOT". Requires `AllowUnsafeBlocks`. `StringMarshalling.Utf8` is first class. Calling convention via `[UnmanagedCallConv]`.
- Best practices: "DO use [LibraryImport], if possible, when targeting .NET 7+"; "DO prefer using function pointers and UnmanagedCallersOnlyAttribute as opposed to Delegate types, when passing callbacks"; "DO use SafeHandle handles to manage lifetime"; "AVOID finalizers"; blittable types (all C# `unmanaged` types when runtime marshalling is disabled) are "simply pinned by the marshaller instead of being copied"; `bool` is not blittable; "CONSIDER using System.Buffers.ArrayPool<T> to pool your native array buffers"; "StringBuilder marshalling always creates a native buffer copy".
- Function pointers: invoking a delegate "uses the callvirt IL instruction. In performance critical code paths, using the calli IL instruction is more efficient"; `delegate* unmanaged[Cdecl]<...>` (csharp unsafe-code). `[UnmanagedCallersOnly]` methods "Must be marked static", "Must not be called from managed code", "Must only have blittable arguments", optional `EntryPoint` export for NativeAOT.
- SafeHandle: "Platform invoke operations automatically increment the reference count of handles encapsulated by a SafeHandle and decrement them upon completion"; it has a critical finalizer and prevents the "recycle attack" (learn SafeHandle).
- Async completion: `TaskCompletionSource<TResult>` "enables the completion of the external asynchronous operation to be propagated to the underlying Task"; all members are thread-safe (learn TaskCompletionSource).
- `GC.KeepAlive` and rooting are required for delegates handed to native code; a `GCHandle` is the documented pattern for a managed object referenced by `user_data` (learn best-practices), which is what pamoja does.
- `[SuppressGCTransition]` (learn SuppressGCTransitionAttribute, fetched 2026-09-30): "When exiting the managed runtime to enter an unmanaged function, the GC must transition from Cooperative mode into Preemptive mode"; suppressing it is allowed only when the native function "always executes for a trivial amount of time (less than 1 microsecond)", "does not perform a blocking syscall", "does not call back into the runtime", "does not throw exceptions", and "does not manipulate locks or other concurrency primitives". Invalid use causes "GC starvation", "Immediate runtime termination", or "Data corruption". This fits request-view accessors (read a header, read the path) and nothing that touches the I/O loop.
- Blittable rule with runtime marshalling disabled (learn best-practices, fetched 2026-09-30): "All types that are C# unmanaged types and don't have any fields that are marked with [StructLayout(LayoutKind.Auto)] are blittable"; `bool` "is passed as a 1-byte value and not normalized". The .NET facade should set `DisableRuntimeMarshalling` so every FFI struct is passed by pointer without a marshalling stub.
- UTF-16 strings are pinned rather than copied only under `StringMarshalling.Utf16`; a UTF-8 P/Invoke argument is converted (learn best-practices). Request views therefore return `ReadOnlySpan<byte>` over Rust memory rather than `string`, and decode on demand.

## 5. Measurements run in this task (2026-09-29 and 2026-09-30)

Machine: Windows 11 Pro 10.0.26200, x64, Node v24.13.0, Python 3.13.1 (GIL build), .NET 10.0.2, cargo 1.96.0. All numbers are single-process, one machine, warm, and are ratios rather than absolutes; the Citrine hardware behind the TechEmpower figures is different. Scripts live next to this file: `bench-napi.js`, `bench_pyo3.py`, `pinvoke-bench/Program.cs`, `bench-napi-roundtrip.js`, `bench_pyo3_roundtrip.py`, `bench-loopback-hop.js`, `bench-probe.js` with `napi-probe/`.

### 5.1 Synchronous call into Rust (bound language calls Rust, same thread)

| Binding | Call | ns per call |
| --- | --- | --- |
| JS baseline | JS function returning a string | 0.5 |
| napi-rs (pamoja `@pamoja/native`) | `version()` returning `String` | 46.5 |
| napi-rs | `encodeDeltaSamples(64 numbers) -> Buffer` | 2,924 |
| napi-rs | `decodeDeltaSamples(Buffer) -> number[]` | 3,436 |
| Python baseline | Python function returning `str` | 28.4 |
| PyO3 (pamoja `_native`, abi3) | `version()` returning `String` | 57.7 |
| PyO3 | `encode_delta_samples(64 ints) -> bytes` | 649 |
| PyO3 | `decode_delta_samples(bytes) -> list` | 558 |
| .NET baseline | managed static method returning `nint` | 1.7 |
| .NET `[LibraryImport]` | `pamoja_version() -> IntPtr` | 4.4 |
| .NET `[LibraryImport]` + `[SuppressGCTransition]` | same | 3.0 |
| .NET `[LibraryImport]` | `pamoja_last_error_message()` (thread-local read) | 4.5 |
| .NET | managed to `[UnmanagedCallersOnly]` through `delegate* unmanaged` | 4.7 |

Reading: a bare crossing costs about 45 ns in Node, about 30 ns above a Python call in CPython, and about 3 to 5 ns in .NET. The expensive part is never the crossing; it is materializing JavaScript or Python values. Converting 64 numbers costs 3 microseconds in Node (65x the bare call), which is why the design in section 6 never hands the bound language arrays or objects it did not ask for.

### 5.2 Async hop (bound language awaits a Rust future, no callback into the bound language)

napi-rs `#[napi] async fn` (pamoja `LoopbackTransport.isConnected()`), Promise resolved on the main thread:

| Pattern | ns per call | calls per second |
| --- | --- | --- |
| sequential await | 26,802 | 37,000 |
| 16 in flight | 2,727 | 366,768 |
| 64 in flight | 2,723 | 367,267 |
| 256 in flight | 2,738 | 365,183 |

Reading: the sequential figure is the Windows cross-thread wake latency (tokio worker to libuv loop and back); it disappears under pipelining. The pipelined floor of about 2.7 microseconds per Promise is the ceiling for any "one Promise per request" design in Node: about 370k requests per second per process before the handler does anything. That is 15 percent of Drogon's Round 23 JSON figure (2,474,350 rps on Citrine, extracted from `round23-ph.json` in this task).

### 5.3 Full round trip (Rust worker thread calls a bound-language handler and waits for its result)

Measured through pamoja's `Transport.fromHandlers` / `PyTransport.from_handlers`, which is the owner's shipped pattern: `#[napi] async fn send` on tokio calls the JS `send` through a `ThreadsafeFunction` and awaits the settled value; Python goes through `future_into_py`, `Python::attach`, `call_method1`, and `into_future_with_locals`. Both hold a per-transport `tokio::sync::Mutex`, so the concurrent columns are serialized by that lock and understate what the mechanism alone can do (the isolated probe in 5.4 removes the lock).

| Binding | Pattern | ns per call | calls per second |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| napi-rs TSFN | sequential | 51,192 | 19,500 |
| napi-rs TSFN | 16 to 256 in flight | 29,124 to 30,001 | 33,300 to 34,300 |
| JS baseline | async fn calling the same handler | 42 | |
| PyO3, sync handler | sequential | 120,232 | 8,300 |
| PyO3, sync handler | 16 to 256 in flight | 79,785 to 88,118 | 11,300 to 12,500 |
| PyO3, `async def` handler | sequential | 194,597 | 5,100 |
| PyO3, `async def` handler | 16 to 256 in flight | 143,341 to 146,474 | 6,800 to 7,000 |
| Python baseline | coroutine calling the same handler | 75 | |

Reading: the shipped pamoja shape, applied naively to HTTP (one TSFN round trip per request, one mutex per transport), would deliver about 1.4 percent of Drogon in Node and about 0.5 percent in Python. Nothing about this is a napi-rs or PyO3 defect; it is the cost of two thread hops plus a lock per request. The handler model must remove the hops from the per-request path, not make them cheaper.

### 5.4 Isolated napi-rs probe (`napi-probe/`, napi 3.13.0, napi-derive 3.6.9, release, thin LTO)

Built in this task to remove pamoja's mutex and measure each primitive alone.

| Primitive | ns per call | Note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `noop()` sync, `u32` return | 13.4 | bare crossing floor |
| `sumSlice(BufferSlice)` 256 bytes | 60.1 | borrowed view, no copy, includes the 256-byte sum |
| `sumOwned(Buffer)` 256 bytes | 118.7 | owned wrapper: `napi_ref` create and delete per call |
| `takeString("/api/users/12345/profile")` | 88.3 | UTF-8 copy into a Rust `String` |
| `reqMethod(&External<Req>)` | 51.5 | opaque handle read returning `u32` |
| `reqPath(&External<Req>)` returning `String` | 88.1 | one JS string materialized |
| `reqHeader(&External<Req>, "user-agent")` | 130.2 | one string in, one string out |
| `makeReq()` returning `External<Req>` | 874.2 | allocation plus finalizer registration |
| `makeBody(1024)` returning external `Buffer` | 858.9 | external buffer plus finalizer |
| `noopAsync()` sequential | 17,647 | cross-thread wake latency |
| `noopAsync()` 64 or 256 in flight | 1,831 to 1,940 | Promise per call: about 520k to 546k calls/s |
| TSFN round trip (tokio worker to JS and back), sequential | 13,620 | 73k calls/s |
| TSFN round trip, 16 in flight | 680 | 1.47M calls/s |
| TSFN round trip, 64 to 1024 in flight | 505 to 533 | 1.88M to 1.98M calls/s |
| TSFN batched, 16 items per crossing, one crossing in flight | 1,136 per item | latency bound |
| TSFN batched, 64 items per crossing | 367 per item | 2.7M items/s |
| TSFN batched, 256 items per crossing | 124 per item | 8.0M items/s |
| TSFN NonBlocking, no return value | 280 | 3.6M calls/s, one-way |

Readings:
- The pipelined ThreadsafeFunction round trip (about 0.5 microseconds) is four times cheaper than a `#[napi] async fn` Promise (about 1.9 microseconds), because the Promise path pays `napi_create_reference`/`napi_delete_reference` and a resolve on the main thread. Rust-owned request flow that calls into JS is cheaper than JS-owned flow that awaits Rust.
- Batching amortizes the crossing: 256 items per crossing costs 124 ns per item, one quarter of the unbatched pipelined cost, and sits inside the 13 ns sync floor plus JS work. A batch of 16 with one crossing in flight is worse than unbatched pipelining, so batching has to be combined with multiple batches in flight, not used alone.
- The single most expensive primitive is creating a finalizable JS object (`External`, external `Buffer`): about 0.87 microseconds each. A request view must not allocate an `External` per request. The design in section 6 uses a per-worker pool of reusable view objects and an integer slot id instead.
- A JS handler that reads three fields (method, path, one header) through the handle costs about 270 ns of crossings, comparable to a single JSON.stringify of a small object (unverified; not measured here).
- Materializing values dominates. The bound language should receive integers and borrowed byte views by default and ask for strings by name only when it needs them.

### 5.5 Isolated PyO3 probe (`pyo3-probe/`, pyo3 0.29.2, non-abi3, release, thin LTO, CPython 3.13.1 GIL build)

| Primitive | ns per call | Note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `noop()` | 22.7 | bare crossing floor (Python call overhead included) |
| `sum_bytes(&[u8])` 256 bytes | 51.5 | borrowed from `bytes`, no copy, includes the sum |
| `take_str(&str)` 24 bytes | 43.4 | UTF-8 borrowed from the `str` object |
| `req.method` getter on a `#[pyclass]` | 33.6 | |
| `req.path` getter returning `&str` | 45.9 | one `str` materialized |
| `req.header("user-agent")` | 55.2 | one `str` in, one out |
| `make_req()` `#[pyclass]` allocation | 200.3 | |
| `make_body(1024)` `bytes` | 110.4 | one copy into the bytes object |
| Rust to Python callback, attached, calling thread | 36 | 27.8M calls/s |
| Rust to Python callback, foreign thread, attach once | 37 | 26.8M calls/s |
| Rust to Python callback, foreign thread, attach per call | 2,249 | 445k calls/s |
| batched 16 / 64 / 256 items per call | 19 / 18 / 16 per item | 52M to 61M items/s |

Readings:
- Under the GIL build there is no thread hop at all: a Rust I/O thread that is attached can call a Python handler in about 36 ns. The cost that matters is `Python::attach` from a foreign thread, about 2.2 microseconds per attach on this machine, which is the price of taking the interpreter per request. A Rust worker must attach once and stay attached while it drains a batch of ready requests, then detach to let other threads run. That is exactly the batching primitive from 5.4, applied to the interpreter instead of the event loop.
- PyO3 object creation is four times cheaper than a napi-rs `External` (200 ns versus 874 ns), so a per-request view object is affordable in Python and not in Node.
- All PyO3 numbers are for the GIL build. The free-threaded build (3.13t) was not installed on this machine, so the concurrent-handler scaling under free threading is unverified here; PyO3's guide says the module must be declared thread-safe and abi3 is ignored on that build (section 3).
- The pamoja host round trip in 5.3 (80 to 195 microseconds) is therefore almost entirely asyncio bridging (`future_into_py`, `into_future_with_locals`, loop wakeups) plus the mutex, not PyO3 call cost. An HTTP handler model must not route each request through asyncio's event loop from Rust; it should call synchronous Python handlers directly on attached workers and reserve the asyncio bridge for handlers that genuinely await.

### 5.6 Isolated .NET probe (`ffi-probe/` C ABI cdylib plus `pinvoke-bench/Program.cs`, .NET 10.0.2, TieredPGO)

| Primitive | ns per call | Note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| native to managed reverse P/Invoke (`delegate* unmanaged[Cdecl]` to `[UnmanagedCallersOnly]`), calling thread | 2.7 | 20M calls |
| same from a fresh native thread, amortized over 20M calls | 2.7 | steady state identical |
| same from a fresh native thread, single call | 12,400 | one-time thread attach to the runtime |
| request view fill (`[LibraryImport]`, struct by pointer, `ReadOnlySpan<byte>` over Rust memory) | 1.3 | below the 2.7 ns delegate-based floor in 5.1, so the generated stub is presumably inlined; reported as measured |
| same with `[SuppressGCTransition]` plus span construction | 1.3 | |
| view fill plus UTF-8 decode of a 24-byte path to `string` | 17.8 | decoding costs 14x the crossing |

Readings:
- .NET has no crossing problem. A Rust I/O worker can call a managed handler for every request at about 3 ns once the worker thread has attached once (12.4 microseconds, paid once per persistent worker). The design constraint in .NET is allocation and GC, not interop.
- An observed pitfall, reproduced here: a `[SuppressGCTransition]` P/Invoke called directly from `Main` binds when `Main` is jitted, before `NativeLibrary.SetDllImportResolver` runs, and throws `DllNotFoundException`. The learn page documents this ("can cause the P/Invoke export to be bound earlier as a side-effect of the calling method being JIT compiled"). The facade must register its resolver in a module initializer or static constructor that runs before any method containing such a P/Invoke is jitted.

Drogon reference for scale: Round 23 JSON 2,474,350 rps, plaintext 14,655,006 rps, fortunes 947,069 rps, single query 1,014,116 rps, 20 updates 454,275 rps; aspnetcore JSON 2,546,481 rps, fortunes 741,878 rps (extracted from `round23-ph.json`; Citrine hardware, 28 hyperthreaded cores, which is not this machine).

## 6. Handler execution model

### 6.1 Rules the measurements impose

1. Nothing per request may cross a thread boundary in Node. One Promise per request caps a Node process at roughly 520k to 546k requests per second on this machine before any handler work (5.4), and one ThreadsafeFunction round trip per request at roughly 2M. Batches of ready requests, several batches in flight, bring the crossing to 124 ns per request.
2. Nothing per request may attach to the Python interpreter. One `Python::attach` per request costs about 2.2 microseconds (5.5); a worker that attaches once and drains a batch pays 36 ns per handler call.
3. Nothing per request may allocate a finalizable JavaScript object. `External` and external `Buffer` creation cost about 0.87 microseconds each (5.4). Request views are slot ids into a per-worker arena, read through accessor calls, with a small pool of reusable view objects per isolate.
4. Values are materialized only on demand. A string in either direction costs 45 to 130 ns in Node and 43 to 55 ns in Python; integers and borrowed byte views cost 13 to 60 ns. The default view exposes `method` as an integer, `path`, `query`, and headers as lazily decoded strings, and the body as a borrowed byte view.
5. .NET is call-per-request with function pointers, `[UnmanagedCallersOnly]` dispatch, blittable `#[repr(C)]` view structs, `DisableRuntimeMarshalling`, and `ReadOnlySpan<byte>` over Rust memory. Its constraints are GC allocation per request and never holding a span past the callback.
6. Whatever can be described as data is executed in Rust without a crossing. That covers most of what TechEmpower measures and most of what the current zero-server users write (static files, JSON from a query, auth rejections, redirects, cached GETs).

### 6.2 Five execution tiers

Tier 0, declarative routes (no crossing). A route is a value: method, path pattern, and one of: a static body with content type and cache headers, a file or directory with ETag and range support, a redirect, a health or readiness probe, a proxy target, a rejection (rate limit, missing or invalid JWT, CORS preflight, body too large). The bound language builds these values and registers them once. Rust owns matching, conditional requests, compression, and the write path. Expected cost: the Rust hot path only.

Tier 1, cached handlers (crossing only on a miss). A handler is registered with a cache spec: key parts (path, selected query keys, selected headers, principal id from the JWT), TTL, stale-while-revalidate window, and an invalidation tag list. Rust serves hits from a per-worker cache (sharded, no cross-thread lock on the hit path) and only misses reach the bound language through tier 3. Invalidation is one call from the bound language (`cache.invalidate(tag)`), which is not on the request path. Expected cost on a hit: tier 0 plus a hash lookup.

Tier 2, data routes (query plans executed in Rust). The bound language describes a query rather than running one: a parameterized SQL text or a query AST built by the facade (the existing zero-server ORM already models tables, relations, casts, and pagination as data, which is the part of the ORM that transfers), parameter bindings from path, query, JWT claims, or validated body fields, and a serialization shape (JSON object, array, template such as fortunes). Rust holds the pool, pipelines the statements, and serializes straight into the response buffer. This is the tier that carries the TechEmpower db, query, update, and fortunes workloads without any bound-language code on the request path. Validation and authorization rules are also data (schema for the body, required claims), evaluated in Rust. Expected cost: the Rust hot path plus the driver.

Tier 3, bound-language handlers, batched. Rust I/O workers accept, parse (HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, later HTTP/3), route, and authenticate. Requests whose route is a tier 3 handler are placed in a per-worker ready queue. A dispatcher moves ready requests to the bound language in batches, with several batches in flight per target, using the mechanism that each runtime makes cheap:
- Node: one ThreadsafeFunction call per batch carrying a batch handle; the JS side iterates slot ids, sets the pooled view object's slot, calls the user's handler, and writes the response through sync accessor calls (`respond(slot, status, headersRef, body)`). A handler that returns a Promise completes later by calling the same sync `respond`; Rust never awaits a JS Promise. Batch size adapts to queue depth (1 under light load for latency, up to 256 under saturation for throughput; 5.4 shows the crossover).
- Python (GIL build): a worker attaches once, drains its batch by calling synchronous handlers directly (36 ns per call), writes responses through `#[pyclass]` accessors, then detaches. A handler declared `async def` is not run on the worker; its batch is posted to a dedicated asyncio loop thread with one `call_soon_threadsafe` per batch, and each coroutine completes by a sync call into Rust. Python users are told plainly that sync handlers are the fast path and that awaiting inside a handler is for genuine I/O that Rust does not already provide.
- Python (free-threaded 3.13t): the same code with several workers attached concurrently; PyO3 0.28 and later assume the module is thread safe, and `#[pyclass]` runtime borrow checking guards view objects (section 3). Wheels are version specific because abi3 is ignored on that build. Scaling on 3.13t is unverified in this task (not installed here).
- .NET: the dispatcher calls one `[UnmanagedCallersOnly]` entry per batch with a pointer to a `#[repr(C)]` batch descriptor (slot ids, view struct pointers). Sync handlers run inline on the native worker thread (persistent, so the 12.4 microsecond attach is paid once). Handlers returning `ValueTask` continue on the thread pool and complete through a function pointer call into Rust. Bodies from managed memory are written with `fixed` pinning for the duration of the write call only; the facade copies into Rust-owned buffers below a size threshold and hands ownership above it.
Body transfer rule for all three: request bodies are borrowed views valid only during the handler call (napi `BufferSlice`, PyO3 `&[u8]`, .NET `ReadOnlySpan<byte>`); a handler that needs the bytes later calls `body.retain()` which copies once into a language-owned buffer. Response bodies are copied into Rust-owned buffers when smaller than 64 KiB (88 ns for a short string in Node, 110 ns for 1 KiB in Python) and transferred by reference above that, with the documented rule that the bound language must not mutate a transferred buffer (napi documents the data race).

Tier 4, Rust plugins. Two forms. In-process crate: the core is a normal Rust library, and a user binary links it and registers `async fn` handlers with the request and response types directly; this is the Drogon-class path and is what the TechEmpower entry uses. Dynamic plugin: a cdylib exposing a versioned `#[repr(C)]` vtable (`zero_plugin_abi_version`, `zero_plugin_register(registry)`) whose handlers receive the same opaque `ZeroRequest` and `ZeroResponse` handles and accessor functions that the .NET binding already uses, so the C header is generated once by cbindgen (pamoja's ffi crate is the template, section 1). The dynamic form pays a C call per request (single-digit nanoseconds) and nothing else. The Rust ABI itself is not stable across compilers, so the dynamic form must stay on the C ABI (unverified here; no source fetched for this statement).

### 6.3 Request view and response builder

- A request lives in a per-worker arena slot for its lifetime; the slot id (u32 generation plus index) is the only thing that crosses. Accessors take the slot id and return integers, borrowed byte views, or a string decoded on demand and memoized in the arena so a second read costs the crossing only.
- The response builder is a Rust object addressed by the same slot id: `status(slot, u16)`, `header(slot, name_id or bytes, value)`, `body_bytes(slot, view)`, `body_str(slot, string)`, `json(slot, bytes)`, `send(slot)`. Common headers are pre-interned integer ids so the hot path passes two integers, not two strings.
- Errors thrown by a handler map to the zero-server error registry (`lib/errors.js` semantics, which transfer as data) inside Rust, so the error response path never makes a second crossing.
- Middleware written in the bound language is a tier 3 handler that returns "next"; middleware that only inspects headers or the JWT is expressed as tier 0 rules instead. Router middleware and query-string mounts from the current zero-server router transfer as routing semantics.

### 6.4 Threads, isolates, and lifetimes per binding

- Node: the Rust core is process-global; each Node isolate (main thread and each `worker_threads` worker) loads the addon, which is context-aware by construction, stores per-isolate state with `napi_set_instance_data`, and registers its own ThreadsafeFunctions (the Node docs forbid sharing `napi_env` across workers, section 2). The dispatcher round-robins batches across registered isolates, so JS handler throughput scales with the number of workers while Rust I/O stays on its own threads. Worker exit runs an env cleanup hook that unregisters the isolate and drains its in-flight batches.
- Python: one Rust core per process; N Rust workers; on the GIL build only one executes Python at a time and the others keep serving tiers 0 to 2; the asyncio bridge (pyo3-async-runtimes `TaskLocals`, already in pamoja) is used only for `async def` handlers and startup hooks, never on the sync path.
- .NET: `SafeHandle` per pamoja `NativeHandle.cs` for server, route table, and cache handles; a `GCHandle` for the dispatch context; no delegates, only function pointers rooted for the process lifetime; `AllowUnsafeBlocks` and `DisableRuntimeMarshalling` assembly-wide; resolver registration in a module initializer (5.6 pitfall).

### 6.5 Facade shape (idiomatic surface, generated contract underneath)

TypeScript: `app.get("/health", ok())`, `app.get("/static/*", files("./public", { etag: true }))`, `app.get("/users/:id", query("select ... where id = $1", { params: ["path.id"], shape: "object" }))`, `app.get("/fortunes", query(..., { shape: template(fortunes) }))`, `app.post("/orders", cached({ ttl: "30s", key: ["path", "auth.sub"] }, (req, res) => { ... }))`, `app.get("/compute", (req) => Response.json({...}))`. Python: decorators mirroring these, sync by default. C#: minimal API style with `app.MapGet("/users/{id}", Query.Object("..."))` and `Func<Request, Response>` handlers; the request type is a `ref struct` over the view.

### 6.6 What transfers from zero-server

Routing semantics and its test suite (router middleware, query-string mounts, mount precedence), the error registry and status mapping, JWT verification and claim rules (executed in Rust), the ORM's model and query description layer (as tier 2 plan builders, not its JavaScript execution), the STANDARDS.md conformance statements as the oracle for the Rust HTTP, WebSocket, and SSE implementations, and the subset of the 8,000 vitest tests that assert observable HTTP behavior, run unchanged against the Node facade the way pamoja runs `conformance.js` against shared vectors. The middleware bodies, the JavaScript ORM adapters, and anything that assumes the handler owns the socket do not transfer.

## 7. Expected throughput by handler language, relative to a Rust handler on the same hardware

These are derived from the per-request costs measured above and are estimates, not measurements of a built system. "Rust" means tier 4 in-process, which is the TechEmpower entry and the target for beating Drogon.

| Handler language and tier | Expected relative throughput | Basis |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Rust, tier 4 in-process | 1.00 | the hot path itself |
| Rust, tier 4 dynamic plugin (C ABI) | 0.98 to 1.00 | one indirect C call per request |
| Any language, tiers 0 to 2 (declarative, cached hit, data route) | 0.97 to 1.00 | no crossing; the cache lookup or plan dispatch is tens of nanoseconds |
| C#, tier 3 sync handler | 0.70 to 0.90 | 3 ns crossing, 1.3 ns view reads, 18 ns per decoded string; the spread is GC allocation per request in the handler body (unverified until a handler corpus is measured) |
| C#, tier 3 async handler | 0.50 to 0.80 | thread pool continuation and completion call; unverified |
| TypeScript, tier 3 sync handler, one isolate | 0.30 to 0.50 | about 124 ns amortized crossing plus 150 to 300 ns of view reads and response calls plus the handler body, all on one JS thread; the JS thread saturates near 1M to 1.5M handler executions per second on this machine while the Rust side is still idle |
| TypeScript, tier 3, N worker isolates | up to 0.80 with 3 or 4 isolates | scales with isolates until the Rust I/O threads or memory bandwidth become the limit; unverified beyond the single-isolate numbers |
| TypeScript, tier 3 async handler (Promise returned) | 0.20 to 0.40 per isolate | adds a microtask and a later `respond` call; never a Rust-side Promise |
| Python, tier 3 sync handler, GIL build | 0.15 to 0.30 | 36 ns call plus 34 to 55 ns per field plus the handler body under one interpreter lock; single core for Python work |
| Python, tier 3 sync handler, free-threaded | scales with workers, per-request cost unchanged | unverified in this task |
| Python, tier 3 `async def` handler through asyncio | 0.05 to 0.15 | batch posting removes the per-request loop wakeup, but each coroutine still pays asyncio scheduling; the naive per-request shape measured in 5.3 is 0.005 |

Two consequences for the product story. First, the throughput number the owner advertises for TypeScript, Python, and C# users is the tier 0 to 2 number, which equals the Rust number, and the documentation should push users toward describing routes and queries as data. Second, tier 3 exists for logic that is genuinely code, and the batching design keeps it in the same order of magnitude as Rust in Node and .NET; Python sync handlers land where a fast Python framework lands today, and Python async handlers should be discouraged on hot routes.
